source.title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence

accepted.question_text: How can a Bayesian or Solomonoff-style account confirm universal hypotheses such as 'all ravens are black' when a natural model uses a parameter θ in [0,1] for the fraction of black objects and standard continuous priors assign prior probability 0 to the universal case θ = 1, causing the posterior probability of the hypothesis to remain 0 even after any finite sequence of black observations?

evidence.quote: a) The zero prior problem. The problem is how to confirm universal hypotheses like H :=“all balls in some urn (or all ravens) are black”. A natural model is to assume that balls (or ravens) are drawn randomly from an infinite population with fraction θ of black balls (or ravens) and to assume some prior density over θ∈[0;1] (a uniform density gives the Bayes-Laplace model). Now we draw n objects and observe that they are all black. The problem is that the posterior proability P[H|black1...blackn] ≡ 0, since the prior probability P[H] = P[θ = 1] ≡ 0.

accepted.question_text: How should confirmation theory resolve the black raven paradox, namely the tension between the claim that observing black ravens confirms the hypothesis that all ravens are black, the logical equivalence of 'all ravens are black' with 'all non-black things are non-ravens', and the apparently absurd conclusion that observing a white sock therefore confirms that all ravens are black?

evidence.quote: b) The black raven paradox by Carl Gustav Hempel goes as follows [Res01, Ch.11.4]: Observing Black Ravens confirms the hypothesis H that all ravens are black. In general, (i) hypothesis R→B is confirmed by R-instances with property B. Formally substituting R❀¬B and B❀¬R leads to (ii) hypothesis ¬B→¬R is confirmed by ¬B-instances with property ¬R. But (iii) since R→B and ¬B → ¬R are logically equivalent, R→B must also be confirmed by ¬B-instance with property ¬R. Hence by (i), observing Black Ravens confirms Hypothesis H, so by (iii), observing White Socks also confirms that all Ravens are Black, since White Socks are non-Ravens which are non-Black. But this conclusion is absurd.

accepted.question_text: How can a theory of induction distinguish the apparently natural hypothesis that all emeralds are green from the rival hypothesis that all emeralds observed until the year 2020 are green and all emeralds observed thereafter are blue, given that both fit the same evidence and that a change of predicates to 'grue' and 'bleen' can make the second hypothesis syntactically simpler than the first?

evidence.quote: c) The Grue problem [Goo83]. Consider the following two hypotheses: H1 :=“All emeralds are green”, and H2 :=“All emeralds found till year 2020 are green, thereafter all emeralds are blue”. Both hypotheses are equally well supported by empirical evidence. Occam’s razor seems to favor the more plausible hypothesis H1, but by using new predicates grue:=“green till y2020 and blue thereafter” and bleen:=“blue till y2020 and green thereafter”, H2 gets simpler than H1.

accepted.question_text: How should the symmetry principle for assigning priors be extended from finite hypothesis classes, where all hypotheses can be taken equally likely, to infinite classes, especially non-compact parameter spaces such as the natural numbers or the real numbers, where classical statistical principles lead to improper distributions that are often unacceptable?

evidence.quote: d) Reparametrization invariance [KW96]. The question is how to extend the symmetry principle from finite hypothesis classes (all hypotheses are equally likely) to infinite hypothesis classes. For “compact” classes, Jeffrey’s prior [Jef46] is a solution, but for non-compact spaces like IN or IR, classical statistical principles lead to improper distributions, which are often not acceptable.

accepted.question_text: In Bayesian confirmation, how should one treat old evidence that is known before the correct hypothesis is formulated, how should the new hypothesis be inserted into the hypothesis class after the fact, what prior should be assigned to it, and to what extent can old evidence confirm the hypothesis rather than merely reflecting that the hypothesis was constructed to fit that already-known evidence?
accepted.context_brief: old evidence and ad hoc hypotheses

evidence.quote: e) Old-evidence/updating problem and ad-hoc hypotheses [Gly80]. How shall a Bayesian treat the case when some evidence E=b x (e.g. Mercury’s perihelion advance) is known well-before the correct hypothesis/theory/model H=b µ (Einstein’s general relativity theory) is found? How shall H be added to the Bayesian machinery a posteriori? What is the prior of H? Should it be the belief in H in a hypothetical counterfactual world in which E is not known? Can old evidence E confirm H? After all, H could simply be constructed/biased/fitted towards “explaining” E. Strictly speaking, a Bayesian needs to choose the hypothesis/model class before seeing the data, which seldom reflects scientific practice [Ear93].

accepted.question_text: How should Solomonoff-style induction be extended or clarified so that it can be compared to Carnap’s confirmation theory and Laplace’s rule, accommodate continuous model classes, and incorporate prior knowledge in a principled way?

evidence.quote: f) Other issues/problems. Comparison to Carnap’s confirmation theory [Car52] and Laplace rule [Lap12], allowing for continuous model classes, how to incorporate prior knowledge [Pre02, Gol06], and others.

accepted.question_text: For a binary sequence whose even-position bits always equal the immediately preceding odd-position bits but whose remaining bits are otherwise incomputable, does Solomonoff prediction eventually exploit that simple computable regularity and predict the even bits correctly from the past, or does it fail in this setting?

evidence.quote: g) Prediction of selected bits. Consider a very simple and special case of problem 5i, a binary sequence that coincides at even times with the preceding (odd) bit, but is otherwise incomputable. Every child will quickly realize that the even bits coincide with the preceding odd bit, and after a while perfectly predict the even bits, given the past bits. The incomputability of the sequence is no hindrance. It is unknown whether Solomonoff works or fails in this situation.

accepted.question_text: Can one identify a nonempty class of 'natural' universal Turing machines or universal semimeasures, or even a single best such machine or semimeasure, that has favorable invariance properties strong enough to control the additive and multiplicative constants that otherwise pervade algorithmic information theory?

evidence.quote: h) Identification of “natural” Turing machines. In order to pin down the additive/multiplicative constants that plague most results in AIT, it would be highly desirable to identify a class of “natural” UTMs/USMs which have a variety of favorable properties. A more moderate approach may be to consider classes Ci of universal Turing machines (UTM) or universal semimeasures (USM) satisfying certain properties Pi and showing that the intersection ∩iCi is not empty. ... A grander vision is to find the single “best” UTM or USM [Müll06].

accepted.question_text: Can one obtain a satisfactory Martin-Löf convergence theory for universal semimeasures in which the relevant universal object still converges to the true measure on Martin-Löf random sequences, with meaningful convergence-rate and convergence-in-ratio results, despite the fact that the standard universal semimeasure M can fail to have Martin-Löf convergence?

evidence.quote: i) Martin-Löf convergence. Quite unexpectedly, a loophole in the proof of Martin-Löf (M.L.) convergence of M to µ in the literature has been found [Hut03c]. In [HM04] it has been shown that this loophole cannot be fixed, since M.L.-convergence actually can fail. The construction of non-universal (semi)measures D and W that M.L. converge to µ [HM07] partially rescued the situation. The major problem left open is the convergence rate for W M.L. −→ µ.
It is also unknown whether convergence in ratio holds. Finally, there could still exist universal semimeasures M (dominating all enumerable semimeasures) for which M.L.-convergence holds.

accepted.question_text: Which generalized classes of semimeasures, Bayesian mixtures over those classes, and corresponding generalized randomness notions yield robust convergence results, and can structural conditions such as denseness characterize when such convergence holds and when it fails?

evidence.quote: j) Generalized mixtures and convergence concepts. Another interesting and potentially fruitful approach to the above convergence problem is to consider other classes of semimeasures M [Sch02b, Sch02a, Hut03b], define mixtures ξ over M, and (possibly) generalized randomness concepts by using this ξ to define a generalized notion of randomness. Using this approach, in [Hut06b] it has been shown that convergence holds for a subclass of Bernoulli distributions if the class is dense, but fails if the class is gappy, showing that a denseness characterization of M could be promising in general.

accepted.question_text: Do lower bounds showing that Solomonoff prediction can assign probability at least 2^{-K(t)} to the wrong next symbol at simply describable times continue to hold after normalizing the universal semimeasure M to a proper measure, or are those bounds merely artifacts of the semimeasure defect of M?

evidence.quote: k) Lower convergence bounds and defect of M. One can show that M(¯xt|x<t)≥2−K(t), i.e. the probability of making a wrong prediction ¯xt converges to zero slower than any computable summable function. ... Do similar lower bounds hold for a proper (Solomonoff) normalized measure Mnorm? I conjecture the answer is yes, i.e. the lower bound is not a semimeasure artifact, but “real”.

accepted.question_text: When AIXI is specialized to a sequence-prediction task, does it predict sequences as well as Solomonoff’s universal prediction scheme even though AIXI does not literally reduce to Solomonoff prediction and the universal prior M is defined on inputs rather than directly on outputs?

evidence.quote: l) Using AIXI for prediction. Since AIXI is a unification of sequential decision theory with the idea of universal probability one may think that the AIXI model for a sequence prediction problem exactly reduces to Solomonoff’s universal sequence prediction scheme. Unfortunately this is not the case. ... The questions is whether, nevertheless, AIXI predicts sequences as well as Solomonoff’s scheme.

accepted.question_text: What notion of universal optimality is both strong enough and still satisfiable for reinforcement-learning agents such as AIXI, and under which formal criteria—such as consistency, self-tuningness, self-optimizingness, efficiency, unbiasedness, asymptotic convergence, finite convergence, or Pareto optimality—does AIXI actually converge to the informed optimal decision maker?

evidence.quote: a) What is meant by universal optimality? A “learner” (like AIXI) may converge to the optimal informed decision maker (like AIµ) in several senses. Possibly relevant concepts from statistics are, consistency, self-tuningness, self-optimizingness, efficiency, unbiasedness, asymptotically or finite convergence [KV86], Pareto-optimality, and some more defined in [Hut05]. ... It is necessary to investigate in more breadth which properties the AIXI model satisfies.

accepted.question_text: For which restricted environmental classes—such as Markov, factorizable, forgetful, relevant, asymptotically learnable, farsighted, uniform, or pseudo-passive environments—can one define and prove general value bounds or optimality properties for AIXI?

evidence.quote: b) Limited environmental classes. The problem of defining and proving general value bounds becomes more feasible by considering, in a first step, restricted concept classes. One could analyze AIXI for known classes (like Markov or factorizable environments) and especially for the new classes (forgetful, relevant, asymptotically learnable, farsighted, uniform, and (pseudo-)passive) defined in [Hut05].

accepted.question_text: Can the AIXI framework be generalized to AIξ for an arbitrary Bayes mixture ξ over a class M of environments in such a way that one can prove relative theorems of the form 'if some policy has a desirable property on M, then AIξ has that property too,' rather than only proving absolute results for specific problem classes?

evidence.quote: c) Generaliztion of AIXI to general Bayes mixtures. Alternatively one can generalize AIXI to AIξ, where ξ(·) = Pν∈M wνν(·) is a general Bayes-mixture of distributions ν in some class M and prior wν. ... The key is not to prove absolute results for specific problem classes, but to prove relative results of the form “if there exists a policy with certain desirable properties, then AIξ also possesses these desirable properties”.

accepted.question_text: Which mathematically precise intelligence-related properties—such as creativity, problem solving, pattern recognition, classification, learning, induction, deduction, building analogies, optimization, surviving in an environment, language processing, and planning—does AIXI satisfy as a rational agent?

evidence.quote: d) Intelligence Aspects of AIXI. Intelligence can have many faces. As argued in [Hut05], it is plausible that AIXI possesses all or at least most properties an intelligent rational agent should posses. Some of the following properties could and should be investigated mathematically: creativity, problem solving, pattern recognition, classification, learning, induction, deduction, building analogies, optimization, surviving in an environment, language processing, planning.

accepted.question_text: For AIXI with an unbounded but slowly growing planning horizon, how fast does the universal posterior M converge to the true environment µ, and can one prove convergence rates strong enough to justify the use of such horizons in the AIXI setting?

evidence.quote: f) Posterior convergence for unbounded horizon. Convergence of M to µ holds somewhat surprisingly even for unbounded horizon, which is good news for AIXI. Unfortunately convergence can be slow, but I expect that convergence is “reasonably” fast for “slowly” growing horizon, which is important in AIXI. It would be useful to quantify and prove such a result.

accepted.question_text: How does the learning speed and quality of AIξ compare with standard reinforcement-learning algorithms such as TD(λ) and Q-learning, especially in environments where AIXI-style elimination of inconsistent environment programs may behave differently from existing efficient algorithms?

evidence.quote: g) Reinforcement learning. ... For Markov environments (but not for partially observable environments) there are efficient general reinforcement learning algorithms, like T D(λ) and Q learning. One could compare the performance (learning speed and quality) of AIξ to e.g. T D(λ) and Q learning, extending [PH06b].

accepted.question_text: Can the key quantities in AIXI and Solomonoff-style reasoning be 'posteriorized' so that posterior weights, complexities, values, and environment probabilities retain the useful properties of their prior versions—particularly a relation between posterior weights and conditional Kolmogorov complexity strong enough to yield practical order-1 bounds?

evidence.quote: h) Posterization. Many properties of Kolmogorov complexity, Solomonoff’s prior, and reinforcement learning algorithms remain valid after “posterization”. ... Strangely enough for wν chosen as 2−K(ν) it is not true that wν(aor<k)∼2−K(ν|aor<k). If this property were true, weak bounds as the one proven in [Hut05, Sec.6.2] ... could be boosted to practical bounds of order 1. Hence, it is highly import to rescue the posterization property in some way.

accepted.question_text: How robust is AIXI to observations that contain irrelevant information, especially when that irrelevant input is complex or non-computable rather than computably generated noise, and under what conditions can AIXI separate such irrelevant input from the information relevant for future observations and rewards?

evidence.quote: i) Relevant and non-computable environments µ. Assume that the observations of AIXI contain irrelevant information, like noise. ... More interesting is the case, where the irrelevant input is complex. If it is easily separable from the useful input it should not affect AIXI. ... How robustly does AIXI deal with complex but irrelevant inputs?

accepted.question_text: In multi-agent settings, especially symmetric two-player situations where each player is an AIXI-type agent observing the other's actions, can one find interesting environment classes closed under such agent-induced environments, and do coupled AIXI or AIξ agents converge to optimal minimax or Nash-equilibrium behavior?

evidence.quote: j) Grain of truth problem [KL93]. Assume AIXI is used in a multi-agent setup [Wei00] interacting with other agents. ... Whereas both AIXIs may be able to learn the game and improve their strategies (to optimal minimax or more generally Nash equilibrium), this setup violates one of the basic assumptions. Since AIXI is incomputable, AIXI(B) does not constitute a computable environment for AIXI(A). ... Many questions arise: Are there interesting environmental classes for which AIξM ∈ M or AIξtlM ∈ M? Do AIXI(A/B) converge to optimal minimax players? Do AIXIs perform well in general multi-agent setups?

accepted.question_text: Can the 'prediction with expert advice' paradigm be extended from passive prediction and active learning to the full reinforcement-learning setting in a way that produces a viable alternative or dual to AIXI, or does the failure of such an extension instead show that AIXI occupies a distinguished position?

evidence.quote: a) Action with expert advice. Expected performance bounds for predictions based on Solomonoff’s prior exist. Inspired by Solomonoff induction, a dual, currently very popular approach, is “prediction with expert advice” (PEA) [LW89, Vov92, CBL06]. ... PEA has been generalized to active learning [PH05b, CBL06], but the full reinforcement learning case is still open [PH06b]. If successful, it could result in a model dual to AIXI, but I expect the answer to be negative, which on the positive side would show the distinguishedness of AIXI.

accepted.question_text: Does treating the agent's actions themselves as universally distributed random variables and then conditioning the universal semimeasure on those actions lead to a meaningful alternative formulation of the generalized universal prior used in AIXI?

evidence.quote: b) Actions as random variables. There may be more than one way for the choice of the generalized M in the AIXI model. For instance, instead of defining M as in [Hut05] one could treat the agent’s actions a also as universally distributed random variables and then conditionalize M on a.

accepted.question_text: What algebraic properties and deeper structural principles characterize AIXI, and can they be distilled into an axiomatic characterization that separates essential assumptions from technical details and thereby guides proofs about the model?

evidence.quote: c) Structure of AIXI. The algebraic properties and the structure of AIXI has barely been investigated. ... It should be possible to extract all essentials from AIXI which finally should lead to an axiomatic characterization of AIXI. The benefit is as in any axiomatic approach: It would clearly exhibit the assumptions, separate the essentials from technicalities, simplify understanding and, most importantly, guide in finding proofs.

accepted.question_text: To what extent is AIXI essentially independent of its defining parameters—such as the observation space, action space, planning horizon, and choice of universal machine—so that the model is unique up to inessential variation rather than genuinely parameter dependent?

evidence.quote: d) Parameter dependence. The AIXI model depends on a few parameters: the choice of observation and action spaces Ø and A, the horizon m, and the universal machine U. So strictly speaking, AIXI is only (essentially) unique, if it is (essentially) independent of the parameters. I expect this to be true, but it has not been proven yet.

accepted.question_text: How does the intelligence order relation compare, both theoretically and on restricted problem classes, to conventional IQ tests and other intelligence or performance measures, and does narrowing the order relation to specific classes of environments reveal principled connections between apparently different domain-specific performance metrics?

evidence.quote: a) General and specific performance measures. Currently it is only partially understood how the IOR theoretically compares to the myriad of other tests of intelligence such as conventional IQ tests or even other performance tests proposed by AI other researchers. Another open question is whether the IOR might in some sense be too general. One may narrow the IOR to specific classes of problems [LH04b] and compare how the resulting IOR measures compare to standard performance measures for each problem class.

accepted.question_text: Can one define a computable, resource-bounded version of the intelligence order relation, or of suitable special cases of it, that yields a practical implementable intelligence test, and which notions of resource-bounded complexity or alternative priors are most appropriate for that purpose?

evidence.quote: b) Practical performance measures. A more practically orientated line of investigation would be to produce a resource bounded version of the IOR like the one in [Hut05, Sec.7], or perhaps some of its special cases. This would allow one to define a practically implementable performance test, similar to the way in which the C-Test has been derived from incomputable definitions of compression using Kt complexity [HO00a]. As there are many subtle kinds of resource bounded complexity [LV08], the advantages and disadvantages of each in this context would need to be carefully examined. Another possibility is the recent Speed Prior [Sch02b] or variants of this approach.

accepted.question_text: Once a computable version of the intelligence order relation is available, what experimental behavior does it exhibit across different problem spaces, does it correlate with human IQ test scores, and in restricted domains such as classification or sequence prediction does it rank algorithms in a way that agrees with standard performance measures and observed real-world performance?

evidence.quote: c) Experimental evaluation. Once a computable version of the IOR had been defined, one could write a computer program that implements it. One could then experimentally explore its characteristics in a range of different problem spaces. For example, it might be possible to find correlations with IQ test scores when applied to humans, like has been done with the C-Test [HOMC98]. Another possibility would be to consider more limited domains like classification problems or sequence prediction problems and to see whether the relative performance of algorithms according to the IOR agrees with standard performance measures and real world performance.
